Hello, I’m Dr. Rivera, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making the time to talk today—caring for a new baby is exhausting enough without extra appointments, so I really appreciate it.

What we’d like to do is a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question form that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally in the past week. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way to make sure we’re giving you the right support during this huge life change.

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause or stop. We’ll go through the questions together, and it usually takes only a few minutes.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Yeah… most of the time I can still laugh. My husband will make a silly joke, or the baby will do something cute and I’ll chuckle. But I have noticed it takes a little more effort—like I have to remind myself to find things funny instead of it just happening naturally like it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before, but I do find myself smiling or giggling once in a while, especially when the baby makes those funny faces while he's sleeping.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hmm… I still look forward to some stuff—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over—but it feels kind of “meh” compared with how excited I used to get. I’ll think, “Oh, that’ll be nice,” rather than really counting down the minutes like I did before the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby was fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy, or I wasn’t holding him the “right” way. I know it’s probably not my fault, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Every now and then I’ll get this sudden wave of worry—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing okay in the crib, even though I just checked on him. It doesn’t last long; I can usually take a breath and calm myself down, but yes, it happens.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, no. I get a little flutter of nerves now and then—like when I’m out walking with the stroller and imagine someone bumping into him—but it’s not a full-blown scared feeling. Just a quick “what-if” that passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

A few times, yeah. Nothing major—just moments when the dishes pile up and the baby wants to cluster-feed and I think, “How am I going to do all this?” I usually manage, but I can feel my chest get tight until I tick one thing off the list.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, nothing like that. I’m tired enough that I usually drop off once I finally lie down—though sometimes it takes me twenty or thirty minutes to settle my thoughts. But my mood hasn’t kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. Not all day or every day, but there are moments—especially in the late afternoon—when I just feel kind of blue and teary for no clear reason. It lifts after a while, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t nap and I felt like I’d tried everything, and once when my partner found a tiny rash on the baby’s chest and I convinced myself I’d done something wrong. It wasn’t an all-day sob fest, just tears that came and went.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I haven’t had any thoughts like that at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety (EPDS-based interview)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Intermittent low mood, tearfulness (“late-afternoon blues”)  
- Reduced pleasure/enthusiasm for previously enjoyed activities  
- Unwarranted self-blame/guilt re infant care  
- Episodic, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety  
- Moments of feeling overwhelmed when multiple demands coincide  
- Two brief crying spells this week linked to infant stressors  

Pattern  
Mild, situational, self-limited symptoms; no persistent anhedonia, no sleep-onset insomnia, no panic attacks, no self-harm ideation.

Risk indicators  
- Subjective sadness and crying (PPD screen positive if ≥2 items)  
- Functional “tight-chest” stress response when tasks accumulate  
- Guilt cognitions re infant well-being (common in postpartum anxiety)

Safety  
Denies any thoughts of self-harm; no further safety concerns identified.

Screening summary  
Patient reports mild mood and anxiety symptoms typical of “baby blues” spectrum, but with preserved capacity for enjoyment, spontaneous laughter, and no impairment of sleep or self-care. Continue routine observation; repeat standardized screening in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms intensify, persist >2 weeks, or function declines.
